To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) the brain infers the likely cause of sensory data, including interoceptive data, by testing it against innate and learned prior beliefs; (b) the ANS is the most important source of interoceptive data; and (c) the ANS can be altered through focused, repeated attention to interoceptive sensations.

(1) the brain is a predictive machine; (2) interoception is the neural signaling from all tissues of our body to the brain; and (3) the brain uses this information to infer our subjective experience of our body and our emotions.

(1) Interoception (the neural signaling to the body from all tissues of our body) is the obvious basis for homeostasis (the regulation of the internal milieu) but some interocepetive signals (from our viscera, muscles and other tissues) rise above this level to contribute to our inferential processes, and thus to our emotional experience.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the relationship between the brain and the body.
the relationship of the body and brain in the generation of emotion, and how this may inform clinical treatment.
the question: How can we best work with the “predictable life” of patients, to facilitate change in psychotherapy?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

(a) interoception is a key factor in the generation of subjective awareness and emotion; (b) interoception can be altered by changing ANS responses, which are in turn influenced by the brain’s predictive processing; (c) the process of mentalizing interoception can provide a route into the patient’s deeply hidden priors, and thus be used to alter habitual ANS responses; (d) this can be used to update dysfunctional responses to emotion, feelings and bodily sensations

the “mentalizing intercep-tion” of the patient’s ANS reflexes, in the safety and privacy of the therapeutic relationship is the best route for the psychotherapist to help patients to change their deeply ingrained prior beliefs.
“mentalizing interocepetion” is a useful concept that may enhance psychotherapeutic practice.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the psychotherapeutic relationship provides the optimal conditions for the patient to learn to “mentalize interoception” and thus to update the priors upon which their habitual responses to emotion and feeling are based.
the most important aspect of psychotherapy is the therapeutic relationship.
the psychotherapeutic process is best served when the therapist is able to “mentalize” their patient’s “interoception.”
The main takeaway from our work is that

, to be effective, psychotherapy must address the interoceptive pri- ors that are the basis of our patients’ emotional reactions, and that this requires a therapeutic relationship that is safe and secure.
the psychotherapeutic relationship can be a safe place for patients to learn to tolerate, and then to “mentalize,” their bodily reactions.
the most effective psychotherapeutic interventions are those that are able to alter patients’ characteristic, habitual responses to emotion and their bodily sensations/reactions to emotional stimuli.
